reports.title: Catching Weiss Crappie from December to March, by Tim Huffman
reports.text:
December and January fishing can be similar in a year with normal, consistent weather. At Weiss, expect fish to be suspended in tributaries and along the main channels.
“Weiss is predominately a white crappie lake,” says Teague. “I find the fish by using my electronics. I start along a channel ledge looking for baitfish. Bait is a key ingredient in the winter, and usually in other seasons, too, but especially the winter. I use Humminbird electronics with Side Imaging being important for scanning areas and then I use a 360 unit on the front. reports.title: CUSA Tournament Winners Adapt to Changing Conditions
reports.text:
Koesters and Hengstler found five weigh-in fish under one dock on the first day but had to fish multiple docks to find the ones holding big fish to finish their limit.
“On day one we started off shooting docks,” said Koesters. “We caught a few good fish over 1.2 pounds. Jake switched to a cork and jig around the docks and landed a 1.88-pound kicker early on day one. After that, we moved to our brush spot in shallow water and caught a 1.98-kicker fish swimming a 1/32-ounce jig in three feet of water. The big black crappies were very shallow. On day two we caught a few fish shooting [docks] but our main crappie came shallow on a cork and jig or shiner.”

reports.title: Advanced Seasonal Structure: Man Made Beds
reports.text:
Placing cover for crappie is nothing new. Stake bed, crappie condo, crappie bed, brushpile, structure and cover are a few of the names fishermen use for these beds. Professional guides, tournament fishermen and serious recreational fishermen have long used the beds to enhance fishing.
Availability is important. Having access to scrap plastic pipe, wood or other material can save hundreds of dollars in costs. Also, wood from the bank is free but sometimes prohibited so the brush may not be available at all. Each type of cover requires some work. The plastic is easiest to assemble and drop. reports.title: Advanced Seasonal Structure Championship Patterns
reports.text:
Jim and Jason Westerberg work a ledge near the mouth of a major arm on Kentucky Lake. Here they are netting a small crappie.
Pattern Number One Fishermen found fish were no on one specific pattern. It was difficult to figure out exactly how to catch fish the bigger fish. The first pattern was a shallow pattern. Fishermen could catch numbers of fish in 2 to 6 feet of water. Pattern one included shallow drops or flats near the drops. Kentucky Lake is literally full of man-made cover, usually stakebeds.
